ClinicalDocument.title: SYNTHETIC RECORD, NOT A REAL MEDICAL RECORD — Cardiology (hypertension and sports cardiology) Consultation — Sonny Liston — True-date frame: synthetic events are moved into the patient's historical lifetime. Codes, instruments, and treatments remain modern and are anachronistic.

code.originalText: Two-week review, seen the same day by cardiology: ambulatory monitoring, echocardiogram, the diagnosis and treatment, and fitness to compete

text.paragraph: High blood pressure readings (154/98 mmHg in the office) in an active professional heavyweight boxer of 37, found at a boxing commission check, with LVH voltage on the ECG. Please confirm and stage the hypertension with the ambulatory monitoring we have arranged, assess for target-organ damage and secondary causes, advise on treatment, and advise on whether and when he can compete. [S]
Urgency: Routine; same day as his two-week primary care visit, after 24-hour ambulatory monitoring next week and an echocardiogram that morning. [S]

list.item: Does ambulatory monitoring confirm hypertension, and at what stage?
Is there target-organ damage, and how do you read the ECG voltage and echocardiogram in a trained heavyweight?
Which secondary causes, if any, should be tested for?
Which treatment do you recommend, and how should it be monitored?
Can he continue to box and compete, and on what conditions?

text.paragraph: Mr. Liston, 37, was seen at the request of Dr. Achebe-Whitford. Everything was explained to him out loud before it was done, and he agreed to each step. He has boxed professionally for many years and trains six days a week with roadwork, bag work and sparring. He was told at a commission check that his blood pressure was high; he has no headaches, chest pain, breathlessness beyond hard sparring, palpitations, fainting or ankle swelling. He snores a little but does not stop breathing in his sleep as far as he knows and is not sleepy in the day (STOP-Bang 2). He takes no medicines, supplements, decongestants, anti-inflammatory pain pills, stimulants or weight-cutting pills. He has cut his drinking from about 25 to about 18 drinks a week over the past two weeks. He does not smoke. [S]
Historical basis. These claims are historical evidence, not findings from a modern examination.

list.item: Charles L. Liston was born in St. Francis County, Arkansas, to sharecroppers Tobe and Helen Liston. His birth date is uncertain: there was no birth certificate (Arkansas did not require them until 1965); he filed for one in 1953 giving May 8, 1932, which the Encyclopedia of Arkansas and the Scribner encyclopedia use with a question; his family's 1930 census record does not list him, so he was probably born no earlier than late 1930; his mother gave several dates; and other sources suggest 1927 or 1928. [D]

He was one of many children (the ninth of his mother's ten; one account counts twenty-two siblings and half-siblings), worked full-time in the cotton fields by the age of eight, and was beaten regularly by his father. [D]
He had virtually no schooling and never learned to read or write. [D]

At thirteen he followed his mother to St. Louis. Arrested in 1950 after a series of robberies, he was sentenced to five years in the Missouri State Penitentiary in Jefferson City, where a Catholic chaplain encouraged him to box; he was paroled in 1952. [D]

He turned professional in September 1953 and broke his jaw in a 1954 loss. He won the world heavyweight title in Chicago on September 25, 1962, with a first-round knockout, and lost it in Miami Beach on February 25, 1964, when he did not come out for the seventh round, citing a shoulder injury; he lost the rematch in 1965. His record was 50 wins (39 by knockout) and 4 losses; he moved to Las Vegas in 1966. [D]
He was described as a heavy drinker and a reckless driver with frequent arrests. [D]

text.paragraph: No results recorded at this visit.

list.item: Hypertension confirmed, stage 2 (I10). Ambulatory averages are well above the thresholds for hypertension (daytime 135/85 and nighttime 120/70 mmHg) and agree with his office readings, so this is sustained hypertension in the stage 2 range, not a white-coat effect. [S]

Mild concentric left ventricular hypertrophy. A wall thickness of 12 mm with normal relaxation can be seen with heavy strength training, but concentric thickening with high ambulatory pressures most likely reflects hypertension, at least in part. It is mild, with normal function and no sign of another cardiomyopathy. A repeat echocardiogram after about a year of control will show whether it regresses. [S]

Secondary causes. Normal potassium, kidney function, urine albumin and thyroid tests, no bruits or radio-femoral delay, and no drugs or supplements that raise blood pressure. Alcohol is the one contributor found, and cutting down should help. Screening for primary aldosteronism is not needed now; it would be if his pressure proved resistant or his potassium fell. A sleep study is not needed with a STOP-Bang of 2. [S]
Alcohol and blood pressure (F10.20). Heavy drinking raises blood pressure, and reducing it is part of his treatment; I support Dr. Achebe-Whitford's plan. [S]

text.paragraph: Data reviewed: 24-hour ambulatory monitoring last week (valid readings 88 percent, including a training session): daytime average 146/94 mmHg, nighttime 132/84 mmHg, 24-hour 142/91 mmHg, nighttime fall 10 percent. ECG at intake: sinus bradycardia 56 per minute, LVH voltage criteria, no ST or T-wave changes, normal intervals. Echocardiogram this morning: mild concentric left ventricular hypertrophy (septum and posterior wall 12 mm), normal chamber size, ejection fraction 60 percent, normal diastolic function (septal e' 10 cm/s), normal valves, aortic root 34 mm. Intake laboratory results as in the referral; urine albumin normal. [S]

list.item: Start a single-pill combination of amlodipine 5 mg and valsartan 160 mg each morning: two first-line drugs, as the 1968 guideline recommends for stage 2 hypertension, with a calcium channel blocker as part of the first combination, and an angiotensin receptor blocker rather than an ACE inhibitor because angioedema is more common with ACE inhibitors in Black patients. [S]
Check potassium and creatinine in two to four weeks; if his pressure is still above 130/80 mmHg at four weeks, raise amlodipine to 10 mg in the same combination. [S]
Home monitoring with a validated upper-arm monitor with a large cuff and a talking, large-number display, two readings each morning sent to the clinic in whatever way works for him. [S]

Avoid diuretics for now, as boxers often dehydrate to make weight; avoid beta-blockers, which blunt exercise capacity and are not first-line; avoid decongestants, anti-inflammatory pain pills and stimulant or weight-cutting supplements. [S]
Lower-salt eating and reduced drinking, alongside his training. [S]
No bouts until his blood pressure is controlled; then clearance by the commission physician with his readings, and a blood pressure check before each bout. He can keep training meanwhile. [S]
Repeat echocardiogram after about a year of control to look for regression of the hypertrophy; lipids, glucose and urine albumin yearly. [S]

Discussed with Dr. Achebe-Whitford, who saw him the same day. The findings were explained to him out loud in two main points (his blood pressure is high and needs a daily tablet; he can train but not fight until it is controlled), and he repeated them back correctly. A letter for the commission physician will be written once his readings are at goal. [S]

Follow-up: Dr. Achebe-Whitford will adjust treatment and check potassium and creatinine at four weeks; cardiology will see him again with the repeat echocardiogram in about a year, or sooner if his pressure stays above goal on two drugs, his potassium falls, or he has chest pain, fainting or palpitations. [S]
